mark_split.label: Identify the reciprocal class and the roots ±1
Divide the quotient by x² and put x + 1/x = t

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.23 — LAQ chapter 2 Theory of Equations, answer 14. Printed appearances: AP 15, 18. THE MARK SPLIT IS THE BOOK'S, with one division of ours inside it: the page prints [2 Marks] beside the two synthetic divisions / 'now we solve the SRE' block, then [1 Mark] each against the substitution, the t values, the roots from t = 5/2, the equation 3x² − 5x + 3 = 0, and its complex roots (2+1+1+1+1+1 = 7); the final 'hence all the six roots' line carries no tag. The card splits the printed 2 as 1 (identify) + 1 (divide), gives the t = 5/3 step the page's 1+1 = 2, and leaves the final list at 0 marks as the page does. The SAME step ids (s1_identify, s2_divide, s3_substitute, s4_solve_t, s5_first_t, s6_second_t, s7_roots) are used on answers 13, 14 and 15, deliberately: one method — remove the root ±1 by synthetic division, then solve the standard reciprocal quotient with x + 1/x = t. The per-step MARKS differ across the three because each page prints its own [N Marks] tags and the card follows its page; a step that the page does not mark separately carries 0 and no red mark. The book writes the substitution letter as y; the card writes t. The book's chapter header carries ★★★; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. Paper position: Maths-2A Section C runs Q18–Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q19 is the Theory of Equations slot (blueprint, book p.3; all five model papers pp.111–120 agree). Model Paper 2 Q19 (book p.114) is this question. Truth check: f(1) = 0 and f(−1) = 0 by substitution; both synthetic-division remainders are 0; the six roots add to 1 − 1 + 2 + 1/2 + 10/6 = 25/6 = −a₁/a₀. The book writes the complex roots first as (5 ± √−11)/6 and then as (5 ± √11 i)/6; the card writes (5 ± i√11)/6 throughout — a notation choice, not a correction. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. No two-book check and no board back-test exist for this paper (no second Maths-2A source in the corpus; answer-book/papers/ holds first-year physics only) — recorded, not hidden. A back-test against the book's own six papers (the five Model Guess Papers plus the Bullet Model Paper, 199 slot-instances) WAS run on 2026-08-29: all 199 resolved to an authored card, and every one carried the section and marks its slot implies. That is a substitute corpus, not a board paper — it cannot show what the board asks that this book omits.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — which roots you take out first and why, how you divide twice, and how the quotient is solved with t = x + 1/x.
insider_note: The x³ coefficient is 0 and must be written in the synthetic division; leaving the column out shifts every later entry.

steps.label: Class II, even degree
steps.margin_note: First mark (the book prints a single [2 Marks] over this step and the next). Even degree; the coefficients 6, −25, 31, 0, −31, 25, −6 change sign end to end: class II, even degree, so BOTH 1 and −1 are roots. Note the missing x³ term is a 0 that must be written.
steps.memory_tip: The signs flip end to end, so this is class II. Even degree, so BOTH 1 and −1 are roots.
lines: Degree n = 6 is even, and aₖ = −aₙ₋ₖ for every k
So this is a reciprocal equation of class II
x = 1 and x = −1 are both roots of it.

recall.must_convey: That the equation is a reciprocal equation of class II and even degree, so x = 1 and −1 is a root for certain, and that this is confirmed by substitution (f(1) = 0).
accept: it is a reciprocal equation of class II and even degree so 1 and −1 is a root, check it by substituting
the coefficient pattern tells you 1 and −1 is a root before you do anything else
first note that x equals 1 and −1 satisfies the equation because of the reciprocal pattern
idi class II and even degree reciprocal equation, kabatti 1 and −1 root avutundi, substitute chesi check cheyyali
the reciprocal class gives the root 1 and −1 with no extra work, verify by putting it in

steps.why: For a reciprocal equation the roots come in pairs x and 1/x. A root that is its own reciprocal must be 1 or −1, and the class (whether aₖ equals aₙ₋ₖ or −aₙ₋ₖ) together with the parity of the degree tells you which of them the equation must contain. Naming it costs one line and saves a whole degree.
common_mistakes: Reading the class from only the first and last coefficients instead of every pair.
Naming only one of ±1 here — this is class II of even degree, so 1 and −1 are BOTH roots.
Not substituting the root back to confirm it, which the examiner expects to see.

steps.label: Divide by (x − 1)(x + 1)
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Two synthetic divisions, one after the other: by 1 (seven coefficients, including the 0 for x³), then by −1 on the quotient. Both remainders must be 0. The final quotient 6x⁴ − 25x³ + 37x² − 25x + 6 is reciprocal.
steps.memory_tip: Two divisions in a row, by 1 then by −1. Write the 0 for the missing x³ or every column shifts.

recall.must_convey: That the polynomial is divided by (x − 1) and then (x + 1) by synthetic division, with zero remainder, leaving the quotient 6x⁴ − 25x³ + 37x² − 25x + 6, which is again reciprocal.
accept: divide by (x − 1) and then (x + 1) using synthetic division, the remainder is zero and the quotient is a reciprocal quartic
synthetic division by (x − 1) and then (x + 1) brings the degree down to four
take out the factor (x − 1) and then (x + 1) by synthetic division and keep the quotient
(x − 1) and then (x + 1) tho synthetic division chesthe remainder zero, quotient reciprocal quartic vasthundi
remove the known root by dividing and work with the quotient

steps.why: The known root is removed by division so that what remains is a STANDARD reciprocal equation of even degree, the only kind the t-substitution handles. Synthetic division also proves the root, because the remainder comes out 0.
common_mistakes: A sign slip in the synthetic division row, so the remainder is not 0 and the quotient is wrong.
Writing the quotient with one coefficient too many or too few (degree must drop by exactly 1 per division).
Dividing by (x − 1) when the root is −1, or the reverse.

steps.label: Put x + 1/x = t
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Divide the quotient by x², group, substitute. 6(t² − 2) = 6t² − 12, and 37 − 12 = 25.
lines: Put x + 1/x = t, so x² + 1/x² = t² − 2

recall.must_convey: That the quotient (a standard reciprocal quartic) is divided by x², and x + 1/x = t with x² + 1/x² = t² − 2 turns it into a quadratic in t.
accept: divide the quotient by x squared, put x plus one by x equal to t, and the squared pair is t squared minus two
the quartic quotient is reciprocal so divide by x square and substitute t
group the quotient into x squared plus one by x squared and x plus one by x then put t
quotient ni x square tho divide chesi x plus one by x ni t ga pettali, t square minus two vasthundi
the quotient becomes a quadratic in t after the substitution

steps.why: The quotient is even-degree and symmetric, so dividing by x² pairs each term with its matching term from the other end and the identity x² + 1/x² = t² − 2 turns four powers of x into one quadratic in t.
common_mistakes: Writing x² + 1/x² = t² and losing the −2.
Forgetting to multiply the leading coefficient into the −2.
Substituting in the ORIGINAL equation instead of the quotient.

steps.label: Solve for t

recall.must_convey: That the quadratic in t is factorised (or solved) to give the two values of t.
accept: factorise the quadratic in t and get the two values of t
solve the t equation by splitting the middle term
the quadratic in t factors and gives two t values
t quadratic ni factorise chesi rendu t values teeskovali
split the middle term of the t equation and read off t

steps.why: The t-equation is a plain quadratic, so factorising it is the cheapest way to the two values of t. Each t value will give two x values, so the count of roots (2 × 2 = 4) is checked here before any x is found.
common_mistakes: A sign slip when splitting the middle term.
Stopping at the two t values as if they were the roots.
Solving the t-quadratic with the formula and making an arithmetic slip a factorisation would have avoided.

steps.label: t = 5/2

recall.must_convey: That t = 5/2 is put back into x + 1/x = t, multiplied out to a quadratic in x, and solved to give the roots 2 and 1/2.
accept: put t equals 5/2 back so x plus one by x is 5/2 multiply by x to get a quadratic and solve it
x plus one over x equals 5/2 gives a quadratic in x whose roots are 2 and 1/2
go back from t equals 5/2 to a quadratic in x and solve
t equals 5/2 ni tirigi x plus one by x lo petti quadratic solve cheyyali
multiply x plus one by x equals 5/2 through by x and use the quadratic formula

steps.why: Each value of t gives two values of x, because x + 1/x = t is a quadratic in x. Solving both t values is what recovers all 6 roots of the original equation — stopping at t answers a different question.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply through by x, so the equation in x is never formed.
Using the quadratic formula on 2x² − 5x + 2 and making an arithmetic slip that the factorisation (2x − 1)(x − 2) would have avoided.
Writing down only one root of the pair: (2x − 1)(x − 2) = 0 gives both x = 2 and x = 1/2.

steps.label: t = 5/3
steps.margin_note: Two marks (the book prints [1 Mark] for forming 3x² − 5x + 3 = 0 and [1 Mark] for its roots). The discriminant 25 − 36 = −11 is negative, so this pair of roots is complex: write √(−11) = i√11.
steps.memory_tip: 25 − 36 = −11 is negative, so write √(−11) as i√11 — this pair is complex.

recall.must_convey: That t = 5/3 is put back into x + 1/x = t, multiplied out to a quadratic in x, and solved to give the roots (5 ± i√11)/6.
accept: put t equals 5/3 back so x plus one by x is 5/3 multiply by x to get a quadratic and solve it
x plus one over x equals 5/3 gives a quadratic in x whose roots are (5 ± i√11)/6
go back from t equals 5/3 to a quadratic in x and solve
t equals 5/3 ni tirigi x plus one by x lo petti quadratic solve cheyyali
multiply x plus one by x equals 5/3 through by x and use the quadratic formula

steps.why: Each value of t gives two values of x, because x + 1/x = t is a quadratic in x. Solving both t values is what recovers all 6 roots of the original equation — stopping at t answers a different question.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply through by x, so the equation in x is never formed.
A slip inside the square root: 25 − 36 = −11, so the root is i√11, not √11.
Dropping this pair because the discriminant is negative — the equation has six roots, and the complex pair (5 ± i√11)/6 belongs in the final answer.

steps.label: All six roots
steps.margin_note: No separate mark on the page for this line, but it is the answer. Six roots for degree 6: 1 and −1 from the two divisions, 2 and 1/2, and the complex pair. Their sum is 25/6 = −a₁/a₀.
steps.memory_tip: Six roots for degree 6, and the 1 and −1 from the two divisions belong in the list.

recall.must_convey: That all 6 roots are listed together — the root(s) removed by division AND the roots found through t: 1, −1, 2, 1/2 and (5 ± i√11)/6.
accept: list all 6 roots together, the one taken out at the start and the ones from t
the roots are 1, −1, 2, 1/2 and (5 ± i√11)/6
do not forget the root removed by division when writing the final answer
anni 6 roots ni kalipi raayali, modata teesina root tho paatu
the final answer collects the roots from both parts of the working

steps.why: The equation was split into a linear factor and a quotient; its roots are the roots of BOTH pieces. The final line is where the removed root is most often forgotten, so it is written out with the others.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the root removed by synthetic division.
Listing the t values among the roots.
Writing a ± pair as one root and so reporting too few roots.
